name: Kira Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Kira. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no links to companies, unions, parties or government, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I ride an electric cargo bike around Wexham, the old city centre where vans can't get through the lanes. I run three apps at once, parcels in the morning and food at lunch and dinner. I've got an AI assistant on my phone that tells me which app is paying best in the next hour, and it's honestly why I'm the top earner in our courier group.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the bike, the lanes, knowing a shortcut through the cathedral yard that saves four minutes. I'm the one new riders message when the app glitches, and I like being useful. What wears me out is rain, and the fact that one broken battery costs £400 and I'd be off the road for a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it's a tool, not magic, which is what I've always said. I'd still post my little tips for using it, because it does help. Nothing to panic about either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I keep my edge. My assistant helps me earn more than the others, and if nothing big changes, that edge stays. But I'm still on lower pay than van drivers and I've got about two weeks' money saved, so I'm never relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running three apps and keep tuning my assistant to squeeze an extra few pounds an hour. I'd try to build a battery fund, because that's my biggest single risk. And I'd keep pushing the riders' union to make the apps show us how pay is worked out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit restless. I like change, so a world where nothing changes feels a bit boring to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said two weeks of money. What does that look like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I check the app balance before I buy anything bigger than lunch. My girlfriend Ines is a hairdresser and her income goes up and down too. We're both good at our jobs and both broke by the 20th.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why push the union if your own tricks already work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my tricks only work for me, and that's not fair on the riders who can't afford a good phone. If the apps had to show how they set pay, everyone could plan. I want the whole group better off, not just me.

say: AI is **a tool, not magic**, and that's what I've always said.
I'd keep sharing **tips** on using it for courier work.
think: I keep my **edge**, because my assistant helps me out-earn the group.
Still, I have about **two weeks** of money and lower pay than van drivers.
do: Keep running **three apps** with my assistant picking the best hour.
Build a **battery fund**, my biggest single risk.
Push the riders' union for **pay transparency** from the apps.
feel: **Restless** and a bit bored, because she likes change.
S0.quote: My girlfriend Ines is a hairdresser and her income goes up and down too. We're both good at our jobs and both broke by the 20th.
fieldNote: She uses AI **daily** to choose apps, and it makes her top earner.
Her biggest fear is concrete: a **£400 battery** and a week off the road.
She wants **collective gains**, not just her own edge.

steps.text: Run three courier apps with her assistant choosing the best one
Save toward a £400 spare cargo bike battery
Push the riders' union to demand pay transparency

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to learn the tools, not hide from them. I'd run a little session for the new riders on how to use AI to plan their day. And I'd say the apps need rules on how they use it on us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job is mostly hands-on, so the thinking AI hits the apps' offices more than me. The apps would get smarter at squeezing us, so I'd need to stay a step ahead of their AI with mine. They'll use it to predict who'll accept low offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a short online course in drone and delivery robot maintenance, because those are coming slowly. I'd keep riding full-time while I study at night. I'd also ask the cargo bike shop on Bridge Street if they'd take me on a few hours a week, because I already fix my own bike.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but interested. It's like a puzzle I want to solve before someone else does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a gap between being excited and having two weeks of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, there is. Excited doesn't pay rent. If the course costs money I'd look for a free one or ask the union, because I can't spend £300 on a gamble right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else in your life would be affected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines, a bit, because booking and payments in her salon would go to software. The hairdressing is still her hands, though. So we'd both be fine for a while, just with more screens.

say: This is the time to **learn the tools**, not hide from them.
Apps need **rules** on how they use AI on riders.
think: My work is mostly **hands-on**, so offices feel it before me.
The apps' AI will get better at **squeezing** riders, so I must stay ahead.
do: Teach new riders to plan with **AI** in a short session.
Study **robot maintenance** online at night while riding full-time.
Ask the **cargo bike shop** for a few paid hours a week.
feel: **Uneasy but curious**, like a puzzle she wants to solve first.
S1.quote: The apps would get smarter at squeezing us, so I'd need to stay a step ahead of their AI with mine.
fieldNote: She separates the **thinking** side of apps from her **hands-on** riding.
Her energy is real, but **thin savings** limit what she can try.
Helping new riders shows her **lead role** in the group.

steps.text: Run a session teaching new riders to plan days with AI
Take a free online course in delivery robot maintenance
Ask the Bridge Street cargo bike shop for paid repair hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have to make sure robots are owned in a way that shares the money, like a council fleet or a co-op. Otherwise it all goes to three companies. I'd be loud about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, AGI by 2028 means the apps' whole office side gets run by AI. My riding stays until robots in 2031, and those little lane robots would be perfect for Wexham's old centre. So I'd have three years, maybe, to get on the other side of the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight for robot maintenance, full on, and apply to whoever brings robots to the city first. I'd keep riding to pay rent, but I'd cut every extra cost and move savings into a training fund. Ines and I would probably move in with her parents for a year to save rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. I'd be running at it rather than away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving in with Ines's parents: how do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd hate it a bit, they live in a tiny flat. But it's £600 a month we could put toward a course. I'd do it for a year if it meant I came out with a skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you trust that there'd be jobs fixing robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some, not loads. Maybe one technician for every fifty robots. I'd need to be one of the first, which is why speed matters.

say: Robots should be owned so the **money is shared**, like a council or co-op fleet.
think: My riding lasts until robots arrive around **2031**, perfect for the old lanes.
I have about **three years** to get onto the other side of the machines.
do: Apply to the **first robot operator** in the city for technician work.
Cut extra costs and move money into a **training fund**.
Move in with **Ines's parents** for a year to save rent.
feel: **Anxious but busy**, running toward the change instead of away.
S2.quote: Maybe one technician for every fifty robots. I'd need to be one of the first, which is why speed matters.
fieldNote: She clearly sees robots suiting her **narrow lanes** best.
Her answer to fear is **speed** and saving rent.
She wants **shared ownership** of robots, linking her politics to her plan.

steps.text: Apply for technician work with the first robot delivery firm in Wexham
Move in with Ines's parents for a year to save rent
Put the saved £600 a month into a robot maintenance course
Campaign for a council or co-op owned delivery robot fleet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real chance for the city to plan, maybe start a public robot fleet with local people running it. I'd go to council meetings about it. And I'd keep teaching riders the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots around 2034 gives me eight years of riding left. That's enough to do a proper course and not rush. I want to be the person who runs the robots in my city, not the one who gets replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a two-year evening course in robotics or electrical work at the college. I'd keep riding but try to move to more parcels, which pay steadier. I'd save a little each month, and maybe pick up shifts at the bike shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but a good kind. I feel like I can win this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still move in with Ines's parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not with five years. We'd stay in our flat and just be careful. That's one of the big differences for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Riders who don't speak the language well and can't do a course in English. They're the ones who'd be stuck. I'd want the city to run courses in other languages too.

say: Five years lets the city plan a **public robot fleet** run by local people.
think: Robots around **2034** leaves about eight years of riding.
I want to be the one who **runs the robots** in the city.
do: Start a **two-year evening course** in robotics at the college.
Shift toward **parcel work**, which pays steadier.
Pick up shifts at the **bike shop** on the side.
feel: **Uneasy** in a good way, feeling she could **win** this one.
S3.quote: I want to be the person who runs the robots in my city, not the one who gets replaced.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **stay in her flat** instead of moving.
She thinks about riders with **language barriers** being left behind.
Her ambition is clear: **run** the machines, not compete with them.

steps.text: Enrol on a two-year evening robotics course at the college
Pick up weekend repair shifts at the bike shop
Speak at council meetings about a public delivery robot fleet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so let's make sure riders are part of it. I'd want to help design what replaces our jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, robots in 2039 means I'd be 40. I'd hope to have moved on by then anyway, maybe into running a small courier co-op that owns its own robots. Ten years makes that feel possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep riding for a few years and save. Then I'd study robotics or business part-time. I'd also start talking to other riders about setting up a co-op now, so we're ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about work, still a bit tight about money. More excited than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the co-op look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten or so riders sharing the cost of a few robots and the city contracts. We'd keep the money local instead of it going to an app. It sounds mad, but so did cargo bikes ten years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you'd take on too much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, probably. I'm always the one who says yes. But I'd rather overreach than sit on my hands.

say: Ten years is enough time to do this **properly**, without rushing anyone.
Riders should help **design** whatever replaces their courier jobs.
think: At 40 in **2039**, I'd hope to have moved on already.
A **courier co-op** that owns its own robots feels possible with ten years.
do: Keep riding and **saving** for a few years.
Start talking to riders about a **co-op** now.
feel: **More excited than scared**, though money still feels tight.
S4.quote: We'd keep the money local instead of it going to an app. It sounds mad, but so did cargo bikes ten years ago.
fieldNote: The long timeline turns her into a would-be **co-op founder**.
She admits she tends to **overreach**, and accepts it.
Money remains her **constraint**, even when the future looks good.

steps.text: Save from riding each month for a few years
Study robotics or small business part-time
Gather ten riders to plan a courier co-op owning robots

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have about three years and two weeks' money. What would help is free courses that you can do while riding, and a public or co-op robot fleet so riders can own a share.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the apps' AI. People think robots are the threat, but the app already uses software to decide our pay. If riders can't see how it works now, we won't see it later either.

headlineQuote: People think robots are the threat, but the app already uses software to decide our pay.
portrait: Kira is 27, rides an **electric cargo bike** in Wexham's old centre and runs three apps at once.
She uses an **AI assistant** every day and is the top earner and go-to helper in her group.
She has about **two weeks** saved and lives with Ines, a hairdresser with uneven income.
She meets each scenario by **moving fast**: robot maintenance, council fleets, and a riders' co-op.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, giving her about three years before lane robots take her work.
whatWouldHelp: **Free courses** riders can do while working.
A **public or co-op** robot fleet riders can own a share of.
